evidence_quotes.quote: This paper synthesizes the evidence on the effectiveness of top-down and bottom-up approaches in providing basic services in slums in developing countries.

For example, the public WSS utility in Kathmandu refused to provide a connection in informal slums, arguing that the households did not have house-ownership certificates. After the NGO’s intervention, the municipal ward committee agreed to act as a guarantor for the two unmetered public taps in the informal slums.

Tenure security is associated with greater disparity in the sanitation services accessible to the poor. Governments are reluctant to take on sanitation projects in illegal or informal slums because doing so would symbolize de facto tenure. Improved sanitation services in notified slums tend to be implemented much faster than in non-notified slums (Chandrasekhar, 2005; Kranthi & Daryani Rao, 2009).

The legal status of the slum determines the type of service provider and the service-delivery approach. This is because government agencies are often restricted in extending coverage to informal slums, as these are considered to be illegal settlements with no security of tenure.

A total of 104 studies formed the evidence base for this review (see Appendix 1, online), comprising 77 for water, 31 for electricity and 64 for sanitation, several of which covered more than one sector. In total, 568 items of evidence were obtained, which were classified as top-down (270) or bottom-up (298) based on the main service provider’s approach, and further classified into five categories:

1. Connectivity: Households with access to basic services  
2. Affordability: Cost of accessing basic services 
3. Adequacy: Availability of the service to its users 
4. Effort and time: Ability to access the services without excess effort and time 
5. Durability: Longevity of the infrastructure facilities created to deliver basic services

criterion_notes.c1: Examines household and community water supply and sanitation service access (alongside electricity) in urban slums across developing countries, synthesizing 77 water studies and 64 sanitation studies out of 104 included studies.
criterion_notes.c2: Under the plain wording of Criterion 2, the study clearly qualifies (yes) because it compares government-led top-down versus NGO/CBO/small-scale private bottom-up institutional and governance approaches to slum basic services. Under the narrow 2026-10-13 rule-type reading, although the overarching top-down versus bottom-up framing includes participatory project-delivery elements, the systematic thematic synthesis and headline findings also directly examine rule-type legal, regulatory, tenure, documentation, and tariff mechanisms governing WSS access — including legal recognition/notification status of slums, land-tenure and house-ownership certificate requirements for utility connections, administrative accommodations (such as municipal ward committees acting as guarantors for unmetered public taps), statutory mandates for WSS utilities to serve unplanned areas, creation of a WSS regulator with a pro-poor legal mandate, regulation of private-sector concessions, municipal demolition enforcement on tenure grounds, and connection-fee/tariff rules — so it passes the narrow reading as well (yes).
criterion_notes.c3: Satisfies Criterion 3 as an explicit systematic empirical synthesis of 104 primary studies (568 coded evidence items) using database/grey-literature searches, EPPI-Reviewer title/abstract/full-text screening, quality appraisal, a structured numerical summary (Table 1), and NVivo line-by-line thematic synthesis (Thomas & Harden, 2008).
criterion_notes.c4: Reports five explicit service-access outcome dimensions across water and sanitation: connectivity (household/community connections), affordability (connection fees and user charges), adequacy (availability, quantity, and quality), effort and time (travel distance, crowding, open defecation), and durability.
criterion_notes.c5: Clearly identifies the population and units of analysis (urban slum households and communities in developing countries synthesized at the study and evidence-item levels across 104 studies / 568 items), the institutional and legal/regulatory exposures, the five multidimensional access outcomes, and the systematic review study design (note: lacks pooled quantitative effect estimates for meta-analysis under synthesis gate Criterion 6, which does not bar systematic-review inclusion).
criterion_notes.c6: Full text is published in English.

study_design: Systematic review (numerical vote-counting summary and qualitative thematic synthesis using line-by-line axial coding)
country: Multiple developing countries (Asia, Africa, Latin America and the Pacific across 104 reviewed studies)
population_and_sample: Urban slum and informal settlement households and communities in developing countries; unit of synthesis is primary empirical studies and extracted evidence items (N = 104 studies — 77 water, 64 sanitation, 31 electricity — comprising 568 evidence items)
exposure: Top-down (centralized government/public utility) versus bottom-up (NGO, CBO, and small-scale private provider / co-produced) service-delivery approaches, alongside rule-type legal and regulatory mechanisms directly governing WSS access (legal recognition/notification of slums, land tenure and house-ownership certificate requirements, ward-committee guarantor accommodations, utility statutory mandates, WSS regulatory creation, private-sector concession regulation, and connection-charge/subsidy rules)
outcome: Household and community access to water supply and sanitation (as well as electricity) evaluated across five dimensions: connectivity, affordability, adequacy, effort and time, and infrastructure durability
rationale: Devkar et al. (2019) is a full-text English systematic empirical synthesis of 104 primary studies (77 water, 64 sanitation, 31 electricity; 568 coded evidence items) examining basic service access in urban slums across developing countries. Inclusion Criterion 3 explicitly encompasses systematic empirical syntheses. While its overarching numerical categorization compares top-down (government/public utility) versus bottom-up (NGO/CBO/private small-scale provider) approaches, its line-by-line thematic synthesis and core findings directly analyze rule-type legal, administrative, and regulatory mechanisms governing water and sanitation access—including legal recognition/notification status of slums, tenure and house-ownership documentation barriers, institutional guarantor accommodations, statutory utility mandates to expand networks into informal areas, creation of a pro-poor WSS regulator, private-concession regulatory gaps, municipal demolition enforcement, and connection-fee/tariff rules—satisfying both the plain wording and the narrow 2026-10-13 rule-type reading of Criterion 2 alongside Criteria 1, 3, 4, 5, and 6.
